name: Monrovia
subtitle: Monrovia, capital of Liberia: its numbers, a short history and places to see beyond the World Heritage list.

keyPoints.text: About 1,760,000 people live in urban Montserrado County (Monrovia, a rounded figure) (counted 2022).
Monrovia is named in honour of James Monroe, fifth president of the United States, and was founded by freed enslaved people who wished to establish a new country in Africa.
The city is built on a cluster of small islands and peninsulas, with lagoons fed by the Mesurado River.

parts.text: Monrovia is named in honour of James Monroe, fifth president of the United States, and was founded by freed enslaved people who wished to establish a new country in Africa.
The city is built on a cluster of small islands and peninsulas, with lagoons fed by the Mesurado River.
Bushrod Island, east of the city centre, holds the capital's deepwater port and most of its industrial infrastructure.
Monrovia has a rainy season lasting from May through October.
In the 1960s improvements to Monrovia's port and ship repair facilities made it home to one of the world's largest fleets of ocean-going merchant vessels.
Monrovia is still recovering from the 2014-15 Ebola epidemic, which prompted foreign investors and companies to leave Liberia and diverted government funds from public investment.
Liberia's urban population grew from 1.63 million in 2008 to 2.86 million in 2022, and the census report names Monrovia and Montserrado County as the principal destinations for migrants.
Monrovia was nearly destroyed in the civil wars: the first Liberian civil war (1989-96) was followed by a second (1999-2003) that further devastated the city.

parts.text: 1,760,000 in 2022, according to the figures compiled from the national statistics office. Which area is counted matters: Monrovia (urban Montserrado County), rounded figure of 1.76 million reported by a fact-check citing the 2022 census thematic report on population projections; the exact LISGIS table could not be read (LISGIS pages need JavaScript).

items.text: In December 1821 the American Colonization Society acquired a strip of coast between the Mesurado and Junk rivers for trade goods valued at US$300.
A small party took possession of Providence Island in the mouth of the Mesurado, and in April 1822 the first permanent settlement was established on the mainland near present-day Monrovia.
Former enslaved people arrived at Providence Island, now Monrovia, in 1822 as part of an American Colonization Society mission.
The National Museum of Liberia was established by President William V. S. Tubman.
Improvements to Monrovia's port made it home to one of the world's largest fleets of merchant vessels.
A civil war broke out between the forces of Samuel Doe and supporters of Charles Taylor.
The second Liberian civil war broke out soon after the first ended and further devastated the city.
The National Museum has been housed in the Old Supreme Court building since 1987.
The Ebola epidemic struck Monrovia and Liberia, prompting foreign investors to leave.
The Monrovia City Council began erecting modern market tables at the Waterside general market.
